questions.q: What is the key difference between a CalloutException and a non-200 status code response?
options: There is no difference — both are thrown as exceptions
A CalloutException means the callout itself couldn't complete; a non-200 status means the callout completed but the remote system reported an error, which does not throw an exception
A non-200 status always throws a CalloutException automatically
CalloutException only applies to SOAP callouts, never HTTP callouts
questions.explain: A CalloutException is thrown for connection-level failures; a non-200 status is a successful HTTP round trip where the error must be checked manually via getStatusCode().

questions.q: Why is a tight synchronous retry loop a bad approach to handling a failed callout in Apex?
options: Because loops are not permitted inside try/catch blocks
Because governor limits (like the per-transaction callout count and cumulative timeout) still apply across every attempt, and it blocks the user for however long retries take
Because CalloutException can never be caught inside a loop
Because HttpRequest objects cannot be reused across iterations
questions.explain: All retries inside one synchronous transaction still count against the same governor limits, and a blocking loop makes the user wait through every attempt.

questions.q: What does the real retry pattern shown in this lesson use to give each retry attempt a fresh set of governor limits?
options: A recursive synchronous method call
Re-enqueuing a Queueable job with a tracked, capped attempt count
Increasing the HttpRequest timeout to the maximum on every attempt
Calling Database.rollback() before each retry
questions.explain: Each Queueable execution runs in its own transaction with its own governor limits, and tracking an attempt count lets the retry be capped rather than running forever.

questions.q: Which kind of failure is generally NOT a good candidate for an automatic retry?
options: A connection timeout to the remote system
A 503 Service Unavailable response
A 400 Bad Request caused by a malformed payload, since the identical request will fail identically every time
A transient network interruption
questions.explain: A 400 Bad Request usually indicates a problem with the request itself; retrying the same malformed request will keep failing and should instead be logged for a person to fix.

questions.q: After the retry attempt cap is reached in the lesson's Queueable pattern, what happens?
options: The job silently stops with no record of the failure
The job throws an unhandled exception that halts the entire org's queue
A durable failure record is created so a human or monitoring process can follow up
The original Order record is automatically deleted
questions.explain: Once the attempt cap is hit, the pattern writes a durable failure record rather than retrying forever or failing silently, giving monitoring (covered in Lesson 23) something to act on.
